# Supplier, cloud and third-party risk {#sec-19-supplier-cloud-third-party-risk}

Chapter 18 governed FastGoods' own riskiest control end to end; Block V closes
with the risk no internal control reaches, because it lives outside the walls.
The moment an organisation uses a supplier or the cloud, part of its security
sits in someone else's hands --- and FastGoods crossed that moment long ago: The
shop runs on a cloud host, card data flows through a payment processor,
marketing mail through an email provider, and the code itself rests on
open-source libraries. This chapter maps the risk that comes with dependence:
What third-party and supply-chain risk is and why accountability never transfers
with the work, the supplier lifecycle of due diligence, tiering and onboarding,
the cloud's shared-responsibility split and the misconfigurations on the
customer's side of it, the contract and the assurance reports that substitute
for controls you cannot configure, and the ongoing oversight --- concentration,
fourth parties, exit plans, the supplier register --- that keeps a checked
supplier a managed one.

## Risk from outside {#sec-19-risk-from-outside}

Modern systems are assembled from suppliers, so an organisation's security is
only as strong as its chain --- suppliers hold your data, run your systems, or
connect into your network, and their weakness becomes your incident. Two related
ideas need keeping apart.

::: {#def-thirdparty}
## Third-party and supply-chain risk

*Third-party risk* is the risk arising from a supplier you use directly ---
their access, their security, their failures. *Supply-chain risk* is the risk
arriving through the chain behind them --- your suppliers' suppliers, the
components inside the software, the platform under the platform. A third party
is anyone you rely on; the supply chain is the whole network behind the service,
and both now belong in any serious risk assessment.
:::

The governing principle of the whole chapter comes first, because everything
else follows from it: *Accountability stays with you*. Work can be delegated;
responsibility for the outcome cannot. The GDPR makes the point statutory ---
FastGoods remains the controller even when a processor causes the breach
(Chapter 7), so "our provider lost the data" is not a defence to Datatilsynet or
to a customer for an R3 incident --- and regulators and customers apply the same
logic beyond privacy: You chose the supplier, you answer for the choice.

The threat side has escalated in a way the history makes vivid. Attackers
discovered that breaching one trusted supplier reaches thousands of its
customers at once --- why attack a company when you can attack its software
vendor and inherit them all? The pattern's milestones: Target (2013), breached
through a heating-and-ventilation contractor's network access; NotPetya (2017),
delivered through a poisoned update of Ukrainian accounting software and causing
billions in collateral damage worldwide; SolarWinds (2020), the definitive case
below; Log4Shell (2021), one flaw in one ubiquitous open-source library becoming
everyone's emergency at once; MOVEit (2023), a single file-transfer product's
vulnerability exploited to extract data from hundreds of organisations that had
merely bought a tool. Trusted suppliers are high-value targets precisely because
they are trusted --- and the practical consequence is that the attack surface
now reaches beyond the walls: Every integration, API key and third-party script
on the checkout page is a potential way in, many dependencies stay invisible
until something breaks, and a surprising number of breaches start at a supplier
the organisation had half-forgotten. Chapter 4's rule returns with new scope:
You cannot protect what you have not mapped --- and the map now includes other
people's companies.

::: {.callout-note}
## Real-world case: SolarWinds (2020): The update as the attack

Attackers --- attributed to Russia's foreign-intelligence service ---
compromised the software *build system* of SolarWinds, whose Orion platform
monitors networks for tens of thousands of customers, and hid a backdoor
(SUNBURST) inside a routine, digitally signed update. Roughly 18,000
organisations installed it in good faith; among the carefully hand-picked
follow-on victims were US federal agencies and major technology firms, and the
campaign ran for months before a security company found it in its own network.
The case defined supply-chain risk for a generation: The victims' own controls
were largely irrelevant, because the poison arrived through the most trusted
channel they had --- the signed vendor update, the one thing patch discipline
says to install. The defences it argues for are this chapter's programme: Know
your suppliers and what they can reach, demand security and transparency of
their build pipelines, monitor as if trust were conditional --- and hold an exit
plan, because the supplier you cannot leave is the supplier whose risk you have
fully adopted.
:::

## The supplier lifecycle {#sec-19-the-supplier-lifecycle}

Supplier risk takes four recognisable forms, and each maps to a control later in
the chapter: *They are breached* --- your data is stolen from their systems;
*they lose availability* --- their outage takes your service down; *they misuse
access* --- excess access is abused or leaked; *they fail or exit* --- the
service stops and you must move fast. Managing them is a lifecycle: Check before
you trust, set expectations in writing, and keep watching.

*Due diligence* is the check before trust, and it scales with what is at stake.
Ask for evidence --- certifications, assurance reports, security policies ---
and match the depth of the check to the sensitivity of the data and access
involved: The payment processor handling card data warrants PCI DSS compliance
and an ISAE 3402 or SOC 2 report read before signing; a low-risk tool needs a
basic check and no more. Record the decision, and any risks accepted with it ---
Chapter 17's register does not stop at the company boundary. Because scrutiny is
finite, *tiering* rations it (@tbl-suppliertiers): Grade suppliers by
the risk they carry, and let the tier set the depth of diligence, the strength
of the contract, and the frequency of review. Onboarding then completes the
entry: The contract signed with the clauses of
@sec-19-contracts-and-assurance, access granted at Chapter 18's least
privilege --- a supplier account is an identity like any other --- and a row
created in the supplier register that @sec-19-managing-it-over-time
maintains.

::: {#tbl-suppliertiers}
  **Tier**    **Criteria**                       **FastGoods example**
  ----------- ---------------------------------- -------------------------------
  Critical    Sensitive data or a core service   Cloud host, payment processor
  Important   Some access or data                Email / marketing provider
  Low         No sensitive access                Office stationery supplier

  : Tiering suppliers by risk: The tier sets how deep the diligence goes, how
  strong the contract must be, and how often the relationship is reviewed.
:::

## The cloud, and who secures what {#sec-19-the-cloud-and-who-secures-what}

Using the cloud means running on someone else's infrastructure with the security
work divided --- not removed --- and the division is where organisations get
caught out.

::: {#def-sharedresp}
## The shared responsibility model

In cloud services, the provider secures what it runs --- the physical data
centres, the network, the virtualisation layer --- and the customer secures what
it controls: Its data, its access, its configuration, and (depending on the
service type) its applications and operating systems. The split shifts with the
service model --- IaaS (rented infrastructure), PaaS (rented platform), SaaS
(rented software) --- but one layer never moves: Your data, and who can access
it, are always yours.
:::

The model reads best as a table (@tbl-sharedresp, after Edwards &
Weaver, Ch. 27), and FastGoods' own case makes it concrete: The shop runs on
rented infrastructure (IaaS), so the provider keeps the data centres, network
and hypervisor --- and FastGoods keeps the customer data and its encryption
(R3), who can log in and with what MFA (R1), and the shop application and its
patching. The running risks sit squarely on FastGoods' side of the line, which
is the point: The cloud is not more or less secure than on-premise --- it is
*differently* secured, and the danger is assuming the provider handles things
that are still yours.

::: {#tbl-sharedresp}
  **Layer**            **IaaS**   **PaaS**   **SaaS**
  -------------------- ---------- ---------- ----------
  Data & access        You        You        You
  Application          You        You        Provider
  OS / runtime         You        Provider   Provider
  Physical / network   Provider   Provider   Provider

  : The shared responsibility model (after Edwards & Weaver, Ch. 27). The split
  moves with the service type; the top row never does.
:::

Two consequences follow, and both are breach statistics. First,
*misconfiguration* --- not clever exploitation --- causes most cloud breaches:
Storage buckets left open to the internet, over-broad permissions, default
credentials, all on the customer's side of the line. A FastGoods bucket
accidentally set public is R3 realised by a checkbox; the Capital One breach of
2019 --- over a hundred million records via a misconfigured access role --- is
the same pattern at scale. Second, the cloud does not do two things people
assume it does: It does not secure *your* configuration and access, and it does
not necessarily back up your data the way you need --- providers guarantee their
infrastructure's uptime, not the recoverability of your records, and resilience
features are often shared or optional. Read what is actually guaranteed; ISO
27001 makes secure use of cloud services an explicit control (A.5.23) for
exactly this reason. Assuming "the cloud handles it" is how an R3 loss becomes
unrecoverable --- Chapter 12's untested-backup lesson, outsourced.

## Contracts and assurance {#sec-19-contracts-and-assurance}

For an internal system you deploy a control; for a supplier you write a clause
--- you cannot configure their systems, so the contract is the primary control,
and weak terms mean weak control. A handful of clauses turn a commercial
contract into a security instrument (@tbl-contractclauses), and one of
them is time-critical in a way Chapter 12 explains: Your own reporting clocks
--- NIS2's 24 hours, the GDPR's 72 --- start running on *your* awareness, so a
supplier who tells you late makes you late; the breach-notification clause is
what connects their incident to your plan. For personal data, much of the table
is not optional: GDPR Article 28 requires the data-processing agreement in
writing (Chapter 7's controller--processor machinery).

::: {#tbl-contractclauses}
  **Clause**              **What it secures**
  ----------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Security requirements   The supplier must meet a defined standard
  Breach notification     They must tell you fast (e.g. within 24 hours) --- your clocks start with their call
  Right to audit          You may audit, or receive an assurance report
  Sub-processors          Limits on passing your data down the chain
  Service levels (SLA)    Agreed availability and response times
  Data processing (DPA)   Required by GDPR Art. 28 for personal data

  : The contract as a control: The clauses that make a supplier's security
  enforceable rather than assumed.
:::

The standards side is compact, because ISO 27001's 2022 revision gathered the
supplier discipline into five adjacent controls --- effectively this lecture in
Annex A form: A.5.19 (information security in supplier relationships), A.5.20
(security within supplier agreements), A.5.21 (managing the ICT supply chain),
A.5.22 (monitoring and reviewing supplier services), and A.5.23 (cloud
services); ISO/IEC 27036 gives the deeper supplier-relationship guidance behind
them. And where auditing a hyperscale provider yourself is impossible,
*assurance reports* substitute: An independent auditor tests the supplier's
controls and you read the result --- ISAE 3402 and SOC 2 being the common
frameworks, in the Type I and Type II flavours Chapter 16 defined. FastGoods
does not audit its cloud host; it reads the host's Type II --- an opinion that
the controls operated all year, the film rather than the snapshot, exactly the
report Chapter 16 taught it to ask for --- and for cloud providers specifically,
the Cloud Security Alliance's control matrix and STAR registry play a similar
role. The regulators, finally, have made all of this duty rather than practice:
NIS2 names supply-chain security among Article 21's required measures, and DORA
goes further for finance --- the register of information, tested exit
strategies, and direct oversight of critical ICT providers that Chapter 15
mapped.

## Managing it over time {#sec-19-managing-it-over-time}

A supplier checked once is not a supplier managed, because suppliers change ---
owners, architectures, subcontractors --- and the clean report read at
onboarding says nothing about their security today. Ongoing oversight runs on
the ISMS's own rhythm (Chapter 3): Re-assess critical suppliers on a schedule,
watch for incidents, ownership changes and new sub-processors, and re-read
assurance reports each year as they are reissued. Two subtler exposures live in
the aggregate view. *Concentration risk*: Too much depending on one provider, so
its outage takes much of you down at once --- CrowdStrike's July 2024, from
Chapter 15, is the canonical morning. *Fourth-party risk*: Your suppliers'
suppliers --- risk you cannot see directly, and the place concentration hides:
If the cloud host, the email service and the analytics tool all run on the same
underlying platform, three contracts share one failure. And because suppliers do
fail, every critical dependency needs a tested exit or fallback --- Chapter 12's
preparedness applied to third parties: Know how you would move off or do without
each critical supplier, keep the data portable and your access to it
contractually guaranteed, and pre-arrange the fallback that keeps the checkout
(R2) selling if the payment provider goes dark. An exit plan is not pessimism;
it is residual-risk thinking pointed outward.

The artefact that holds it all is one page (@tbl-fgsuppliers): Every
supplier, its service, its tier, its assurance, and the standing action --- the
register that turns this chapter from a lecture into a routine.

::: {#tbl-fgsuppliers}
  **Supplier**        **Service**       **Tier**    **Assurance**   **Action**
  ------------------- ----------------- ----------- --------------- ---------------
  Cloud host          Runs the shop     Critical    SOC 2 Type II   Review yearly
  Payment processor   Card data         Critical    PCI DSS         Review yearly
  Email provider      Marketing mail    Important   Self-attested   Spot-check
  Stationery          Office supplies   Low         None needed     None

  : The FastGoods supplier register: Tier drives assurance, assurance drives the
  action --- and the empty cells are as deliberate as the filled ones.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Finding the risk: In the supplier register

Read the register backwards, the way every register in this course gets read.
Suppliers missing from it entirely --- the analytics script marketing added, the
free SaaS tool a team adopted --- are unmanaged access wearing no row at all;
shadow suppliers are found by walking the invoices and the browser's network
tab, not the contracts folder. Then the rows themselves: A critical-tier
supplier with self-attested assurance is a contradiction in terms; an assurance
report more than a year old is Chapter 16's snapshot problem, aged; a contract
without a breach-notification clause is a reporting clock you cannot start; and
three rows resolving to one underlying platform is concentration risk filed
under three names. Each finding converts straight into Chapter 8's register ---
source, event, consequence, with the supplier as the source.
:::

::: {#exm-studentcloud}
## The student's third parties

The dependence is already yours: The thesis lives in a cloud drive, the
references in a citation service, the code on a hosting platform --- free tiers
all, guaranteeing little. Run the chapter on them. Shared responsibility: The
provider keeps the service up; the account security (Chapter 18's MFA) and the
decision to export are yours. Concentration: If the "backup" is the same
account's sync folder, original and copy share one takeover --- Chapter 8's
thesis risk, rediscovered as fourth-party thinking. Exit: Can you export
everything, today, in a usable format? Try it once --- the download that fails
in the test is Chapter 12's untested backup with a vendor's logo on it. Twenty
minutes, three suppliers, one register row each: The lecture, at personal scale.
:::

##### Reading for this chapter.

Edwards & Weaver, Chapter 7 (risk management, with the supply-chain attack
surface, pp. 109 ff.) and Chapter 27 (cloud security and the shared
responsibility model, pp. 481 ff.). Standards and law: ISO/IEC 27001:2022,
A.5.19--A.5.23 (the supplier controls) with ISO/IEC 27036 behind them; NIS2,
Article 21 (supply-chain security as a required measure); DORA, Articles
28 ff. (ICT third-party risk, the register of information, oversight of critical
providers). Both books are available in the library and on the Canvas course
page.

## Summary {#sec-19-summary}

Dependence is the modern default, and its rule is absolute: Accountability stays
with you --- GDPR's controller logic generalised --- while the work moves out.
Third-party risk is the supplier you chose; supply-chain risk is the chain
behind them (@def-thirdparty), and the attack pattern from Target
through NotPetya, SolarWinds, Log4Shell and MOVEit shows why trusted channels
are the target of choice: One compromise, thousands of victims, with the signed
update as the weapon. Suppliers are managed as a lifecycle --- due diligence
scaled to sensitivity, tiering that rations scrutiny
(@tbl-suppliertiers), onboarding with least-privilege access and a
register row. The cloud splits security rather than removing it
(@def-sharedresp): The provider keeps its infrastructure, the customer
always keeps data and access, and the breach statistics live on the customer's
side --- misconfiguration first --- while two assumptions ("they secure it",
"they back it up") stay false until the contract says otherwise (A.5.23). Where
you cannot configure, you contract (@tbl-contractclauses) --- breach
notification feeding your own clocks, audit rights, sub-processor limits, the
Article 28 DPA --- and where you cannot audit, you read assurance: The ISAE 3402
/ SOC 2 Type II, Chapter 16's film, with A.5.19--A.5.23, NIS2 Article 21 and
DORA's third-party pillar making the discipline law. Over time, oversight runs
on the ISMS rhythm: Re-assessment, reissued reports, concentration and
fourth-party awareness, a tested exit per critical dependency, and the one-page
supplier register (@tbl-fgsuppliers) holding it together.

Block V is complete: Audited, evaluated, one risk governed end to end, and the
outside dependencies brought under the same discipline. Block VI raises the
ceiling --- starting with the question every executive eventually asks: Can we
put numbers on this? Qualitative and quantitative risk, Lecture 20.

## Self-check {#sec-19-self-check}

Try these before the next lecture.

::: {#exr-19-draw-the-line}
## Draw the line

FastGoods moves the shop from IaaS to a hosted webshop platform (SaaS). Using
@tbl-sharedresp, list what moves to the provider's side, what stays on
FastGoods' --- and name the one risk of R1--R3 whose ownership does not change
at all.
:::

::: {#exr-19-tier-and-check}
## Tier and check

A new AI-chatbot service wants read access to order history to answer customer
queries. Assign its tier, list the due-diligence evidence you would demand
before onboarding, and name the two contract clauses that are non-negotiable.
:::

::: {#exr-19-race-the-clock}
## Race the clock

FastGoods' email provider suffers a breach on Friday 18:00 and notifies
FastGoods on Monday 09:00; customer data was exposed. Explain what this delay
does to FastGoods' GDPR position (Chapter 7's clock), and write the contract
clause that would have prevented the problem.
:::

::: {#exr-19-find-the-concentration}
## Find the concentration

FastGoods' register shows: Cloud host (platform X), email provider (runs on
platform X), analytics tool (runs on platform X), payment processor (own
infrastructure). Name the exposure, the incident from this course that
illustrates it, and one measure that reduces it without leaving platform X
entirely.
:::

::: {#exr-19-test-the-exit}
## Test the exit

Write the three-line exit test for the payment processor: What FastGoods must be
able to do, the evidence it works, and the R2 consequence if the test has never
been run.
:::
